claims.text: Substitutional alloying with elements of varying atomic radii introduces controlled lattice distortion in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
This substitutional-alloying intervention can simultaneously enhance strength and ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
A balanced composition gives eutectic high-entropy alloys optimal mechanical properties.
The lattice distortion must remain moderate to avoid loss of alloy stability or formation of unwanted precipitates.
Temperature and cooling rate can be optimized to retain the desired microstructure.
Lattice distortion can cause the formation of defects such as dislocations.
The introduced defects interact with one another and with the microstructure to enhance both strength and ductility.
Substitution-induced lattice distortion strengthens the alloy by creating additional obstacles to dislocation motion.
Controlled introduction of defects improves ductility by enabling more efficient plastic-deformation mechanisms.
The intervention will increase yield strength by at least 10% relative to the baseline alloy.
The intervention will improve ductility by at least 15% relative to the baseline alloy.
The appropriate baseline is a compositionally balanced, optimally processed eutectic high-entropy alloy without intentional lattice-distortion alloying.
The hypothesis should hold for eutectic high-entropy alloys having moderate to high entropy of mixing.
The hypothesis should hold at temperatures and strain rates relevant to structural applications.

Yield strength, ductility, lattice distortion, and microstructure can be compared between substitutionally alloyed samples and a baseline using mechanical testing, X-ray diffraction, and transmission electron microscopy.
